newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek government says won't bow to blackmail.
newsitem.headline: Greek government says won't bow to blackmail.

text.p: Greece's socialist government said on Monday it would not bow to blackmail by thousands of farmers who have blockaded national road and rail links for 12 days.
"The government cannot and will not surrender to blackmail. It is obliged ... to secure the working of the economy and the state," National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou told reporters.
Farmers, with a list of economic demands, have paralyzed road and rail links, blocking nearly 100 points around Greece and causing chaos for international and domestic transport.

"I'm carrying fresh meat," French driver Malique Adadee told Reuters Television in the farm town of Larissa. "I don't know what to do. I've been trapped for a week. They should at least let foreign drivers pass so that we can go home."
Hundreds of lorries are trapped around Greece. Drivers must stay with trucks -- despite food, water and sanitation problems -- for fear of cargoes being stolen.
Borders with Bulgaria and Turkey have been closed and Athens has been cut off by land from Greece's second city of Salonika in the north.
On the Bulgarian side of the border the blockade has caused a two-km (1.2-mile) traffic jam. Trucks have been stranded with no food and tonnes of perishable products like milk and meat.
"Vehicles have been stuck at the border for more than a week waiting for the lifting of the blockades on Greek territory," said Valentin Tsenev, a Bulgarian police officer at the border.
But farmers, who have erected increasingly elaborate camps in the middle of Greece's roads, have vowed to stay put until Christmas or beyond unless the government gives in.
"We are determined to stay on the roads for as long as the government wants to keep us here," said Yannis Pattakis, leader of the Larissa farmers' union -- the heartland of the rebellion.

He said the government was grossly exaggerating the cost of the farmers' demands, which he put at 130 billion drachmas ($520 million). That is the same sum the socialists hope to make after sweeping away an array of tax breaks in 1997.
With neither the government, which is struggling to meet European Union economic targets, nor the farmers backing down, Greeks are bracing for food shortages before Christmas.
So far, however, the farmers have carefully avoided blocking the rich agricultural area around Thebes, north of the capital, or stopping produce arriving from the island of Crete.
"The farmers are being cautious and tactically smart. They are not cutting off the capital because they don't want public opinion against them," said political commentator John Loulis.

Prices of fresh fruit, vegetables and meat have risen in the main Athens market but not dramatically. There have been none of the scenes of acute shortage which occurred in a similar 10-day farmers' blockade in March 1995.
Loulis said at the moment there was a stand-off, with the government hoping public opinion would turn against the farmers and the farmers hoping public opinion would turn against the government.
"But so far the government has failed to convince the vast majority of Greeks that its economic measures are socially just or that they will be effective," he said.
The government announced new taxes and the abolition of tax breaks last month along with its 1997 budget, which is seeking to bring the economy in line with Greece's EU partners.

The measures have sparked a stream of marches through Athens by workers. Teachers, students, construction workers, pensioners and housewives have marched. Even Greek diplomats are refusing to work after losing their main tax break.
